title: The Bobo Doll
text:
In the early 1960s, Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross at Stanford University brought 72 children from the university nursery school, aged three to six, into a playroom one at a time. In the corner stood an adult playing with toys, including a large inflatable clown called a Bobo doll.

For some children, the adult ignored the doll and played quietly. For others, after a minute, the adult attacked it: sitting on it, punching it in the nose, hitting it with a wooden mallet, tossing it in the air and kicking it around the room, while saying things like "Sock him in the nose" and "Pow." A third group saw no adult at all.

Afterward, each child was taken to another room with attractive toys, told they could not play with them after all, and then led to a room that included a Bobo doll and a mallet. Children who had watched the aggressive adult were far more likely to attack the doll, and many copied the adult's exact blows and words. Children who had seen the quiet adult were even less aggressive than the control group. Boys copied physical aggression more than girls, especially from a male model.

The study became a cornerstone of social learning theory.
lesson: Children copy what they see us do, often in precise detail, far more than what we tell them. Your own behavior is the lesson.
people: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, Sheila Ross
source: Bandura, A., Ross, D., and Ross, S. A. (1961). Transmission of aggression through imitation of aggressive models. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 63(3), 575-582.
caveat: Critics note that hitting a toy designed to be hit is not the same as aggression toward people, so the study speaks more clearly about imitation than about real violence.
